# FinShield for OpenCode Desktop

[Product GitHub](https://github.com/finogeeks/finsafe) · [Safety Arena](https://safety.finaios.ai/) · [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@finogeeks2026/finshield-opencode)

**Let your agent work. Keep its access under control.**

Agents can do more than delete files: they can access private information, disrupt your desktop and change system settings. FinShield adds Windows sandbox protection to OpenCode Desktop's execution backend, helping keep agent operations within configured access boundaries while you keep your usual coding workflow.

See what those boundaries can mean in practice:

## Requirements

- Windows x64.
- OpenCode Desktop V2. The integration currently targets OpenCode Desktop/SDK 2.3.0.
- An internet connection to download the plugin and its native components.

Install [OpenCode Desktop](https://opencode.ai/) first if you do not already have it.

## Install

With the OpenCode V2 CLI installed, run:

```sh
opencode plugin add @finogeeks2026/finshield-opencode
```

Restart OpenCode Desktop to load the plugin. Desktop only? See [Install without the CLI](#install-without-the-cli).

## What happens on first launch

FinShield automatically prepares its components and configures Windows sandbox permissions in the background. This can take a while; you can keep using OpenCode while it finishes. Windows may ask for administrator consent.

When ready, FinShield prompts you to exit and reopen OpenCode. After that, protection starts automatically on normal launches. You can check its status at any time in **Settings > FinShield**.

## Update

Use **Check for updates** on the FinShield settings page. After an update finishes, save your work, exit OpenCode and open it again manually. Check the current protection status after reopening.

## Troubleshooting

### Install without the CLI

Add FinShield to `plugins` in `%USERPROFILE%\.config\opencode\opencode.json`, keeping your other settings and plugin entries:

```json
{
  "plugins": ["@finogeeks2026/finshield-opencode"]
}
```

If the folder or file does not exist, create it. If you already use `opencode.jsonc` or a custom configuration directory, edit that configuration instead. Restart Desktop; OpenCode downloads and loads the configured plugin automatically. See [OpenCode's plugin documentation](https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins/).

### FinShield does not appear in Settings

Confirm that you edited the global configuration used by this Desktop installation, that the field is `plugins` for V2, and that the package name is `@finogeeks2026/finshield-opencode`. Check for JSON errors and plugin download or load errors before repeating installation.

### The plugin is installed but protection is not active

Check **Settings > FinShield** for preparation progress or an error. When preparation is ready, exit and reopen OpenCode as prompted to activate protection.

## Scope and license

This Windows integration protects the backend Host and retains Desktop Main. Network mode is `host`; do not interpret the AppContainer integration as a claim of complete network isolation. See the product's compatibility and verification documentation for the current supported scope and remaining acceptance limits.

## Startup

Double-click OpenCode normally. Plugin setup returns without waiting for the
updater, download, installation, authorization or page. Management errors remain
visible in Settings > FinShield. The current Host token determines protection.
After setup, choose Exit OpenCode or Later. The next normal start uses the
existing startup handoff to replace Host and retain Main. The native connection
must reach that Host before startup handoff completes.
A protected session shows its current state in Settings.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[OpenCode native startup] --> B[Desktop available]
    A -.Plugin activation.-> U[OpenCode updater]
    U --> E[Prepare target and offer Exit or Later]
    E --> M[User closes and opens OpenCode manually]
    M --> H[Startup AppSeam handoff retains Main]
    H --> C[Native recovery reconnects the existing Desktop]
```

## Build and package

For npm-style local experience, use the committed
`docs/local-npm.md` in the source checkout. It serves the plugin,
matching SDK and native installer, then prints the normal `opencode plugin add`
command. It does not install the plugin or launch OpenCode for the user.

Generate the bundled Candidate from the product manifest when configuration
sources change. Run these commands from this directory:

```powershell
npm ci --ignore-scripts
npm run build:policy
npm run build
npm pack --ignore-scripts --pack-destination C:\owned-test
```

The package carries JavaScript, Candidate and notices. The independent updater
uses OpenCode's installed Bun runtime; users need no additional Node or Bun
installation. The declared SDK carries Koffi and the common product DLL. For development
before the matching SDK is published, build and pack it with the
SDK build instructions in `sdk/node/README.md` in the source checkout and install from that
local archive.

Install the archive in an owned package directory and add its installed package
directory to OpenCode's global `opencode.json`:

```json
{"plugins":[{"package":"C:/owned-test/packages/node_modules/@finogeeks2026/finshield-opencode"}]}
```

Managed native versions use `%ProgramFiles%\FinSAFE\opencode-plugin-versions\<version>`.
Configuration uses `%ProgramData%\FinSAFE\opencode-plugin-versions\<version>\config`.
The security domain is `finshield.opencode`. The product sources live under
`windows/config/opencode-plugin/`. The install rule covers the stable parent
read-only. The generated Candidate is under `policy/`.
Downloads and updater stages use their own `opencode-plugin` and
`opencode-updater` locations under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\FinSAFE`.

The updater installs and authorizes the selected version through the shared SDK.
During an update it stages the existing desired Candidate. An exact match for
the prototype default selects the formal bundled Candidate for the new version.
The matching FinSAFE executable supports
`app launch opencode --retain-main PID:CREATED --replace-host PID:CREATED`. Plugin removal retains native runtime,
configuration and authorization.

OpenCode's configuration is the only user configuration entry. The plugin derives
native and configuration paths from its requested release and Windows known
folders. Manual native executable, YAML and version-root overrides are retired.
It does not read or write `finsafe-windows/config.json`, migrate an old snapshot,
or save runtime process and resource data. The updater keeps an explicit update
target in memory; installation registration and authorization remain native-owned.

## Verify

Use the plugin-owned driver and read its plan first:

```powershell
python test/verify.py --lane unit --lane native --lane page --dry-run
python test/verify.py --lane unit --lane native --lane page
```

The former external-instance `installed` lane is retired. Set
`FINSHIELD_OPENCODE_SDK_ARCHIVE` for a verification run with a locally packed SDK.
The final-stage `product` lane uses the normal plugin installation flow, opens
an owned Windows shortcut, observes the actual token/native connection/session
and checks unchanged shared file hashes. It requires a declared disposable
Windows test account and its own authorization; do not run it on a working desktop.
The `policy` lane uses an explicit compatible FinSAFE executable and temporary
files only. Final-stage `product`, `lifecycle` and `isolation` need their stated

Cross-native-version authorization reuse, model/MCP/network cases, full crash
and multi-window recovery remain unaccepted. Network mode is `host`. The SDK

# FinSAFE Node SDK

The public SDK carries `bin/finsafe_native.dll`, built by the personal edition's
existing CLI package from Prepare, Execution, Installer and AppSeam modules.
DSH and OpenCode declare this SDK as a dependency. Their archives use its
product DLL. The SDK owns Koffi 3.1.1 and bundles its Windows x64 native package.
Importing the SDK loads no DLL or Koffi native addon.

```js
import {createClient} from '@finogeeks2026/finsafe-sdk';
const call = createClient();
const identity = await call({module: 'prepare', request: {action: 'identity'}});
```

`loadKoffi()` is the public lazy entry for existing direct Windows bindings.
Both this entry and `createClient()` resolve Koffi from the SDK package. Plugins
must not resolve it from a host or inspect the SDK's private dependency paths.
Windows locks a loaded native addon. On first native use, the SDK synchronously
copies its two dependency directories to a unique `finshield-sdk-koffi-*`
directory under that process's standard temporary directory, then loads from
there. Later calls in the same SDK module reuse the loaded instance. This
bounded copy is about 2.83 MB; it preserves the synchronous call API and allows
package removal while a Host remains alive. It is required loading work, not a
startup precheck. Failure is reported directly. Copies are not shared between
processes or used as persistent state. Native mappings last until the process
exits; remaining temporary files use the system's normal temporary-file cleanup.
The SDK adds no cleanup process, service, shared cache or locks.
`createClient({libraryRoot})` supports an explicit removal-safe copy of the SDK
library without changing dependency resolution. An optional `require` injection
is retained for controlled tests. The default library is this SDK's
`bin/finsafe_native.dll`. This is independent of the operation's installation
and configuration targets, which callers pass explicitly. First installation
uses the same product Installer operations without needing a prior full install.

Scope: native dependency ownership. Parent: plugin delivery. Input: an SDK
package. Output: native calls or the original loading error. The updater copies
the complete SDK, including bundled dependencies. No host Koffi is required.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    D[DSH plugin] --> S[Node SDK]
    O[OpenCode plugin] --> S
    S --> K[SDK-owned Koffi]
    K --> L[Product DLL and existing Windows bindings]
```

Koffi adds two delivered packages on Windows x64: `koffi` and
`@koromix/koffi-win32-x64`, with no further runtime dependencies. Their installed
files total about 2.83 MB in 3.1.1. The SDK archive includes their MIT licenses.
The native component is an optional dependency for platform selection, but is
required when using this Windows x64 SDK. Publication verifies its presence.
The shared updater source owns orchestration, not dependency installation.

Named product modules are `prepare`, `execution`, `installer`, `desktop` and the explicit
AppSeam adapters `app_seam.dsh` and `app_seam.opencode`. Application compatibility stays in AppSeam; Core
never selects behavior from application identity. Product modules own native
handles, singletons and process lifetimes. The SDK only adapts calls and callbacks.
Cancel exit observation before releasing its Node callback. Native cancellation
waits for queued callbacks; a failed cancellation retains the callback.

Build the product DLL with `python scripts/prod/build-node-sdk.py` from the
repository root. Run `npm install --package-lock=false --ignore-scripts` and then `npm pack` from this
directory on Windows x64. Publication on another build host stages dependencies
with `--os=win32 --cpu=x64` before packing. Consumers install the
prebuilt package without Rust. Public release signs the product DLL before npm
packaging and publishes the SDK before exposing the dependent DSH Git package, market index
or npm package.

## Common HTTP status client (#1163)

DSH, OpenCode and Kilo use the package-owned SDK to call the selected shell backend's new
HTTP resources. The [canonical query contract](../../docs/internal/design/plugin-updater-shared.md#unified-sdk-http-status-queries-1163-2026-11-22)
defines authorization state, attempt-bound progress, application status, optional
installation/update reads and resource events. `createStatusClient` exports
`authorizationState`, `authorizationProgress(attempt)`, `applicationStatus(id)`,
`applicationInstallation(id)`, `applications`, `update` and `subscribe`.
Each query issues an independent HTTP request. Each subscription has its own
stream and cancellation. There is no query-result or pending-request cache,
subscription sharing, saved endpoint discovery or request replay.
`createAuthorizationObserver` has been removed.

```js
const connection = await obtainShell(selectedSettings);
const status = createStatusClient(connection);
const state = await status.authorizationState();
// Later queries use this connection; they do not invoke obtainShell again.
```

Load the complete SDK from the plugin's own dependency directory. Delivery
pins the packages; runtime loading does not compare package versions, DLL
versions or source commits. Native load errors are returned directly.

`obtainShell(settings)` is the common public launch adapter for DSH, OpenCode
and Kilo. Each invocation calls the native launch owner with the explicit
executable, Effective YAML and user environment. Shell alone decides start,
reuse or replacement through its existing algorithm. The SDK returns its actual
`origin` and authenticated `nonce`, or distinct cancellation or actual error.
It keeps no completed result, Promise or endpoint cache. Timeout does not kill
the Shell or replay the request. The native owner lets a new Shell inherit the
requesting updater's Job, so it ends with that session. Obtaining an existing
Shell does not transfer its Job or lifetime. Releasing only the request does
not end Shell. Accepted native authorization keeps its separate lifetime.

Background entry requests no Widget or Console display. It otherwise uses the
same Shell, identity, HTTP, update and Inspector behavior as foreground entry.
Query calls use the returned connection and neither start Shell nor fall back
to CLI, DLL status reads or installation discovery. The former signed-discovery
client and authorization observer have been deleted. The updater owns the live
connection for its selected target. When updater A explicitly selects B, it
installs B and obtains Shell B while keeping its own A SDK. FinSAFE B executes
B configuration and authorization. Queries for B use Shell B.

Use `python scripts/dev/verify.py --lane dsh-windows-plugin` for Node/packaging
checks and `--lane dsh-windows-updater` for native product fixtures. Those fixtures
change no installed product or authorization. SDK publication is a separate
release operation; this change does not publish an npm version.

# Overview

Koffi is a fast and easy-to-use dynamic C FFI module for Node.js, featuring:

* Low-overhead compared to a static Node-API implementation (see [benchmarks](https://koffi.dev/benchmarks))
* Support for primitive and aggregate data types (structs and fixed-size arrays), both by reference (pointer) and by value
* Support for synchronous and asynchronous calls
* Javascript functions can be used as C callbacks
* Well-tested code base for popular OS/architecture combinations

The following combinations of OS and architectures __are officially supported and tested__ at the moment:

ISA / OS           | Windows     | Linux/glibc | Linux/musl  | macOS       | FreeBSD     | OpenBSD
------------------ | ----------- | ----------- | ----------- | ----------- | ----------- | --------
x86 (IA32) [^1]    | ✅ Yes      | ✅ Yes      | 🟨 Probably | ⬜️ *N/A*    | ✅ Yes      | ✅ Yes
x86_64 (AMD64)     | ✅ Yes      | ✅ Yes      | ✅ Yes      | ✅ Yes      | ✅ Yes      | ✅ Yes
ARM64 (AArch64) LE | ✅ Yes      | ✅ Yes      | ✅ Yes      | ✅ Yes      | ✅ Yes      | 🟨 Probably
RISC-V 64 [^2]     | ⬜️ *N/A*    | ✅ Yes      | 🟨 Probably | ⬜️ *N/A*    | 🟨 Probably | 🟨 Probably
LoongArch64        | ⬜️ *N/A*    | ✅ Yes      | 🟨 Probably | ⬜️ *N/A*    | 🟨 Probably | 🟨 Probably

[^1]: The following call conventions are supported: cdecl, stdcall, MS fastcall, thiscall.
[^2]: The prebuilt binary uses the LP64D (double-precision float) ABI. The LP64 ABI is supported in theory if you build Koffi from source but this is untested. The LP64F ABI is not supported.

Go to the web site for more information: https://koffi.dev/

provided by Node.js when using C++. It provides a C++ object model
and exception handling semantics with low overhead.

# node-api-headers - **[Introduction](#introduction)** - **[Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md)** - **[Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)** - **[Install](#install)** - **[API](#api)** - **[Creating a release](CREATING_A_RELEASE.md)** - **[Team](#team)** - **[License](#license)** ## Introduction **node-api-headers** contains the header files for the C-based Node-API provided by Node.js. Node-API is an API for building native addons that guarantees the ABI (Application Binary Interface) stability across versions of Node.js (see: [Node-API](https://nodejs.org/dist/latest/docs/api/n-api.html)). Node-API headers are in the `include` folder. The Node-APIs that provide ECMAScript features from native code can be found in `js_native_api_types.h` and `js_native_api.h`. The APIs defined in these headers are included in `node_api_types.h` and `node_api.h`. The headers are structured in this way in order to allow implementations of Node-API outside of Node.js considering that for those implementations the Node.js specific APIs may not be applicable. **node-api-headers** is also a package published on **npm** that could be used in a process to compile and build native addons for Node.js. ## Install ``` npm i node-api-headers ``` ## Versions Node-API C headers are backward-compatible. Its version (e.g. `8`) is released separately from the Node.js version stream (e.g. `19.8.1`) and changes are backported to active Node.js LTS lines (e.g. `16.x` and `18.x`). This package publishes semver-minor versions with new Node-API C headers changes. JS API breaking changes are published with new semver-major versions. ## API The module exports two properties `include_dir` and `symbols`. ### `include_dir` This property is a string that represents the include path for the Node-API headers. ### `def_paths` This property is an object that has two keys `js_native_api_def` and `node_api_def` which represents the path of the module definition file for the `js_native_api` and `node_api` respectively. ### `symbols` This property is an object that represents the symbols exported by Node-API grouped by version and api types. ```js V1: { js_native_api_symbols: [ // List of symbols in js_native_api.h for the version 1. ], node_api_symbols: [ // List of symbols in node_api.h for the version 1 ] }, // ... ``` ## Team members The project is maintained by the [Node-API team members](https://github.com/nodejs/abi-stable-node/?tab=readme-ov-file#project-participants). ## License Licensed under [MIT](./LICENSE.md)

# OpenCode Windows plugin architecture

## Reuse OpenCode's runtime (#1189, 2026-11-25)

The owner approved reusing OpenCode's installed runtime for the independent
updater. The ordinary plugin Host supplies its current executable through
`process.execPath`. AppSeam starts that executable outside the Host replacement
tree, with `BUN_BE_BUN=1` in that child process's environment. This uses Bun's
[documented standalone CLI mode](https://bun.sh/docs/compiler/executables#act-as-the-bun-cli).
The child executes the staged `updater/server.js` and its existing arguments.
The updater removes the mode variable before starting any management or Host
work, so normal OpenCode launches do not inherit Bun CLI mode.

Scope: updater components. Parent: native desktop plugin activation. Inputs:
the ordinary Host executable and this release's staged package. Output: an
independent ordinary updater using the delivered SDK. Launch errors retain the
existing diagnostic and status path. Invariants: no new startup precheck,
runtime download or global Node dependency; no Core, authentication, Job,
authorization, manual reopen or protected-Host bootstrap changes.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P[OpenCode plugin] -->|Installed OpenCode runtime| U[Independent updater]
    U --> S[Package-owned common SDK]
    S --> N[Existing native operations]
```

The package contains no Node executable or `node-win-x64` dependency. Staging
keeps the complete SDK and release directory contract. An old
`opencode-updater/runtime/node.exe` is ignored and left untouched; it is not a
fallback. The common transport retains its existing `node` executable field
for compatibility with its other callers. No DSH implementation is copied.
An updater already running from the previous release retains its existing
lifetime. Manual close/reopen starts the new updater with the Host runtime.

Research on 2026-11-24 used installed OpenCode Desktop 2.3.2, whose backend
contains Bun 1.4.4. A separate backend process executed external JavaScript,
loaded package SDK 0.11.50 and Koffi 3.1.1, and completed synchronous FFI and
asynchronous native build-info calls. The delivered SDK DLL's Authenticode
signature was valid. These are runtime compatibility probes, not clean-profile
installation, updater lifecycle or protected-session acceptance. Other OpenCode
versions still require acceptance; do not add an inferred version admission gate.
Compiled Bun executables built without CLI support cannot use this mechanism;
report their actual launch error instead of installing another runtime.

Changed artifacts must use a new coordinated plugin/SDK/native release version.
Published 0.11.50 bytes and existing version stages remain immutable. Source
development and owned fixtures do not authorize npm publication or user setup.

## Plugin independence

Formal Windows builds use `dev/build_release.py` to stage the package, install
locked development dependencies, build the GUI and updater, and bundle the
source-matched public SDK. The shared public-plugin renderer supplies the release
CDN base. Both the full Actions release and the local Windows release publish
this built package after the matching native release and SDK.
Native installation uses the shared verified download in `updater/common/download.js`:
CDN and the same version's public GitHub Release start together; the first
verified result wins and cancels the other source. Local npm preview overrides
only its staged package's CDN base.

Local preview delivery uses the plugin-owned [npm preview workflow](docs/local-npm.md).
It stages package copies and serves immutable artifacts over loopback. This
development tool changes no sandbox or platform capability; the platform matrix
needs no additional change for the delivery tool.

OpenCode uses its own application adapter and the declared product SDK.

The Node updater flow is owned by `integrations/common/windows` and delivered
in this plugin's archive. OpenCode declares the FinSAFE Node SDK for native
calls and has its own application adapter, Candidate, runtime namespace and UI. The
SDK carries the personal-edition product DLL. The plugin package carries no
Rust build or private DLL.

## Available package updates

Owner-approved revision, 2026-11-23, #1170. OpenCode owns package installation
and plugin loading. Only the loaded plugin supplies the native target version.
This revision supersedes the earlier OpenCode install-only update sequence in
the shared manual reopen contract. DSH keeps its existing sequence.

Scope: one OpenCode package update. Parent: plugin management. Inputs: the
configured package source and the user's update action. Outputs: actual package,
loading and native preparation results. Errors remain with their stage. Normal
startup and the current Host's protection do not depend on update completion.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C[OpenCode checks the installed FinShield package] -->|New version available| N[FinShield shows an update notification]
    N -->|User selects Update| U[OpenCode updates the package]
    U --> L[OpenCode loads the new plugin]
    L --> P[Loaded plugin synchronizes FinShield]
    P --> R[Show actual results and manual reopen instructions]
```

DSH lets its host manage the package update. OpenCode uses the built-in server's
plugin inventory, check and update APIs for the same responsibility. FinShield
checks its configured package on launch, periodically and on request from its
settings page. A notification offers Update or Later. The host applies the
configured source and version rules. Checking does not change the package or
touch the native installation. Update starts only after user confirmation.

The old plugin finishes after `plugin.update()` returns. It does not read
`plugin.list()` to infer the native target or submit native installation.
Package completion is not plugin activation. If OpenCode does not load the new
plugin in this session, the user closes and reopens manually first. Loading
failures retain the host's error; no native task for the unloaded plugin starts.

The loaded server module reads its package version V once. Management
`version()` returns `{version: V}` without starting or waiting for an updater or
Host attachment. Status also reports this module version, independently of old
Host feedback. Host management objects are shared only within the same immutable
release, so B cannot inherit A's activation closure or SDK. Desktop attachment
uses the existing verified Main and Host inputs.

Parent node: `Loaded plugin synchronizes FinShield`. Inputs: the loaded package,
its delivered SDK, explicit roots and the existing updater channel. Output: the
native preparation task for V, or its original error. Plugin registration does
not wait for native installation or authorization.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    V[Loaded module supplies its own version V] --> B[Bind using its SDK and explicit roots]
    B --> E[Submit existing ensure operation for V]
    E --> M[Existing updater installs and authorizes FinShield V]
    M --> R[Report preparation result and manual reopen requirement]
```

In a protected session, B connects to the existing ordinary A updater. That
updater keeps its own A runtime and SDK while executing the B installation and
authorization task. Its own version is not the target. No updater replacement,
SDK hot replacement, new ordinary process or version-negotiation flow is added.
Normal ordinary startup still creates a fresh updater through the existing
acquisition operation. Plugin activation always uses the normal managed flow.

Existing `ensure` handles same-version state and full preparation. The
install-only acknowledgment is not completion or authorization success.
The page distinguishes package completion, the loaded server module version,
native work and its errors, and current Host protection. Window-local handoff
data keeps only the package notice; it does not select the native release.
Exit stops OpenCode without relaunching it. If a reopen was needed to load B,
another reopen can still be needed to activate prepared FinShield B.

V is passed unchanged to settings and management. Stable releases use the same
three-part version for plugin, bundled SDK and FinShield. Local suffixes are
not stripped to claim alignment: the existing stable-only native delivery
contract reports its error until a separate suffixed-release contract is
defined. Complete package staging and explicit version roots remain unchanged;
OpenCode cache generations are never scanned for a target.

## Configuration and removal

The product owns `windows/config/opencode-plugin/manifest.yaml`. Resolve
generates the packaged `policy/candidate.yaml` from the OpenCode base, Windows
mandatory rules and the existing OpenCode compatibility source.
Native versions are separate children of `opencode-plugin-versions`. The read-only
install rule covers their stable parent. Resolve/Materialize must produce equal
authorization inputs for a version-directory change. Actual native upgrade
receipt reuse still requires installed acceptance.

During setup, a byte-for-byte match for the original prototype Candidate
selects the bundled formal Candidate for the new version. Staging keeps edited
Candidates and leaves the active installation's configuration in place.

Native management uses the plugin's own domain, `finshield.opencode`, for product
setup or authorization. Development fixtures leave `finsafe.shared` unchanged.
Real setup requires the final-stage disposable Desktop test environment.

OpenCode's Extensions switch controls GUI only. Native negative-ID configuration
controls server loading. Removing the package entry releases its management
binding; the current protected Host, runtime, configuration and authorization
remain. Native uninstall is rejected before dispatch. No native uninstall driver
or implementation is part of this plugin.

### Koffi 3.0

#### Koffi 3.0.2

*Released on 2026-05-26*

- Fix unexpected type error when passing array of pointers (see [Koromix/koffi#269](https://github.com/Koromix/koffi/issues/269))
- Search more native addon directories under `process.resourcesPath`
- Rearrange Koffi loading to use `require()` for static packages
- Avoid declare module syntax in TypeScript definition file
- Fix error when using *String* array hint with UTF-32 string types (`const char32_t *`)
- Add *Buffer* array hint to convert arrays and pointers to Node Buffer objects
- Reduce overhead of various Koffi functions

#### Koffi 3.0.1

*Released on 2026-05-20*

- Fix error when importing default koffi module from TypeScript
- Optimize creation of new JS objects for return values
- Adjust build flags for performance

#### Koffi 3.0.0

*Released on 2026-05-16*

**Highlights:**

- Rewrite call preparation and execution for **vastly improved performance**
- Distribute prebuilt binaries in **separate subpackages**

**Breaking changes:**

- Replace use of externals with type objects:
  * Use `koffi.type()` to resolve type specifiers (strings or objects) to type objects
  * Access type information directly on type objects without `koffi.introspect()`
- Replace use of externals with BigInt pointers

**Other changes:**

- Support ESM and CJS module types
- Add `koffi.enumeration()` to create [enum types](input#enum-types)
- Add fast decode functions for integers, floats and strings
- Use proper types for various objects and handles:
  * Use *LibraryHandle* objects for loaded libraries
  * Use *TypeObject* objects for Koffi types
  * Use *PollHandle* for socket poll handles
- Add `Symbol.dispose` on library objects and poll handles
- Prefer types to interfaces in TypeScript declaration file
- Fix various bugs and small leaks (such as library handles)
- The ARM32 backend has been temporarily removed

**Newly deprecated functions:**

- Deprecate `koffi.resolve()` function, replace with `koffi.type()`
- Deprecate `koffi.introspect()` function, replace with `koffi.type()`

**Removed deprecated functions:**

- Remove `koffi.callback()` long replaced with `koffi.proto()`
- Remove `koffi.handle()` long replaced with `koffi.opaque()`

Consult the [migration guide](migration) for more information.

## On virtual machines

Koffi is tested on multiple architectures using emulated (accelerated when possible) QEMU machines. First, you need to install qemu packages, such as `qemu-system` (or even `qemu-system-gui`) on Ubuntu.

The Linux machines are based on Debian, they are not included in the repository but they can be created at any time with the scripts in `tools/cross/build`. For example, to create the Debian ARM64 machine, use the following commands:

```sh
cd tools/cross/build
./debian_arm64/build.sh
```

The other machines (Alpine, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, macOS and Windows) are created manually, at least for now. These machines are not included directly in this repository (for license and size reasons), but they are available here: https://download.koromix.dev/qemu/

For example, if you want to build and test for Windows, run the following commands:

```sh
cd tools/cross/
wget -q -O- https://download.koromix.dev/qemu/qemu_windows_x64.tar.zst | zstd -d | tar xv
```

Note that the machine disk content may change each time the machine runs, so the checksum test will fail once a machine has been used at least once.

And now you can run the tests with:

```sh
cd src/koffi

node tools/brew.js test # Several options are available, use --help
```

And be patient, this can be pretty slow for emulated machines. The Linux machines have and use ccache to build Koffi, so subsequent build steps will get much more tolerable.

Machines are started for each test if needed, and stay active until you stop them. You can start and stop them at any time with the following commands:

```sh
node tools/brew.js start # Start all available machines
node tools/brew.js stop # Stop everything
```

You can also restrict these commands to a subset of machines:

```sh
# Full test cycle
node tools/brew.js test debian_x64 debian_i386

node tools/brew.js start debian_x64 debian_i386
node tools/brew.js test debian_x64 debian_i386
node tools/brew.js stop
```

Each machine is configured to run a VNC server or SPICE, which you can use to access the display, using KRDC or any other compatible viewer. Use the `info` command to get the VNC or the SPICE port.

# Code style

Koffi is programmed in a mix of C++ and assembly code (architecture-specific code). It uses [node-addon-api](https://github.com/nodejs/node-addon-api) (C++ N-API wrapper) to interact with Node.js.

My personal preference goes to a rather C-like C++ style, with careful use of templates (mainly for containers) and little object-oriented programming. I strongly prefer tagged unions and code locality over inheritance and virtual methods. Exceptions are disabled.

Find more information about code style in the [monorepository README](https://codeberg.org/Koromix/rygel/#c-flavor) file.

# Settings

## Memory usage

For synchronous/normal calls, Koffi uses two preallocated memory blocks:

- One to construct the C stack and assign registers, subsequently used by the platform-specific assembly code (1 MiB by default)
- One to allocate strings and objects/structs (2 MiB by default)

Unless very big strings or objects (at least more than one page of memory) are used, Koffi does not directly allocate any extra memory during calls or callbacks. However, please note that the JS engine (V8) might.

The size (in bytes) of these preallocated blocks can be changed. Use `koffi.config()` to get an object with the settings, and `koffi.config(obj)` to apply new settings.

```js
let config = koffi.config();
console.log(config);
```

The same is true for asynchronous calls. When an asynchronous call is made, Koffi will allocate new blocks unless there is an unused (resident) set of blocks still available. Once the asynchronous call is finished, these blocks are freed if there are more than `resident_async_pools` sets of blocks left around. By default, the preallocated stack and heap blocks are much smaller than for synchronous calls (see [default settings](#default-settings)).

> [!CAUTION]
> The **memory usage can blow up easily** if you increase the size of async memory blocks and many async calls are running or queued at the same time !
>
> For example, with 4096 running/queued async calls, a stack size of 256 kiB and a heap size of 512 kiB, the memory usage will reach approximately _4096 * (256 + 512) kiB ≈ 3 GiB_ just for Koffi, even though most of it will be freed once the number of queued calls goes down.

Async calls run on worker threads, the number of which depends on the number of cores in your machine. Additional async calls are queued, up to `max_async_calls` can run and be queued at the same time. If you try to make an async call once the queue if full, an exception will be thrown.

## Default settings

Setting              | Default | Maximum | Description
-------------------- | ------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------
sync_stack_size      | 1 MiB   | 16 MiB  | Stack size for synchronous calls
sync_heap_size       | 2 MiB   | 16 MiB  | Heap size for synchronous calls
async_stack_size     | 128 kiB | 16 MiB  | Stack size for asynchronous calls

# POSIX error codes

You can use `koffi.errno()` to get the current errno value, and `koffi.errno(value)` to change it.

The standard POSIX error codes are available in `koffi.os.errno`, as shown below:

```js
const assert = require('assert');

import koffi from 'koffi';
// CJS: const koffi = require('koffi');

const lib = koffi.load('libc.so.6');

const close = lib.func('int close(int fd)');

close(-1);
assert.equal(koffi.errno(), koffi.os.errno.EBADF);

console.log('close() with invalid FD is POSIX compliant!');
```

# Reset internal state

You can use `koffi.reset()` to clear some Koffi internal state such as:

- Parser type names
- Asynchronous function broker (useful to avoid false positive with `jest --detectOpenHandles`)

This function is mainly intended for test code, when you execute the same code over and over and you need to reuse type names.

> [!WARNING]
> Trying to use a function or a type that was initially defined before the reset is undefined behavior and will likely lead to a crash!

Koffi also accepts BigInt values when converting from JS to C integers. If the value exceeds the range of the C type, Koffi will convert the number to an undefined value. In the reverse direction, BigInt values are automatically used when needed for big 64-bit integers.

Koffi defines a few more types that can change size depending on the OS and the architecture:

C type           | JS type          | Signedness  | Note
---------------- | ---------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------
bool             | Boolean          |             | Usually one byte
long             | Number (integer) | Signed      | 4 or 8 bytes depending on platform (LP64, LLP64)
ulong            | Number (integer) | Unsigned    | 4 or 8 bytes depending on platform (LP64, LLP64)
unsigned long    | Number (integer) | Unsigned    | 4 or 8 bytes depending on platform (LP64, LLP64)
intptr           | Number (integer) | Signed      | 4 or 8 bytes depending on register width
intptr_t         | Number (integer) | Signed      | 4 or 8 bytes depending on register width
uintptr          | Number (integer) | Unsigned    | 4 or 8 bytes depending on register width
uintptr_t        | Number (integer) | Unsigned    | 4 or 8 bytes depending on register width
wchar_t          | Number (integer) | | 2 bytes on Windows, 4 bytes Linux, macOS and BSD

Primitive types can be specified by name (in a string) or through `koffi.types`:

```js
// These two lines do the same:
let struct1 = koffi.struct({ dummy: 'long' });
let struct2 = koffi.struct({ dummy: koffi.types.long });
```

# String types

Koffi can convert JS strings to and from UTF-8, UTF-16 or UTF-32.

Type name                      | Aliases         | JS type | Conversion / encoding
------------------------------ | --------------- | ------- | ---------------------
const char \*, char \*         | str, string     | String  | UTF-8
const char16_t \*, char16_t \* | str16, string16 | String  | UTF-16
const char32_t \*, char32_t \* | str32, string32 | String  | UTF-32

Koffi also supports wide strings (`wchar_t *` or `wstring`), which use:

- UTF-16 on Windows (where wchar_t is 2 bytes)
- UTF-32 on other platforms (where wchar_t is 4 bytes)

# Enum types

*New in Koffi 3.0*

C enumeration values are stored as integers. The underlying integer type is implementation-defined but Koffi tries to match usual platform behavior.

On POSIX platforms, Koffi follows the following rules:

- If no negative value exists: `unsigned int` by default, `uint64_t` if needed
- If any negative value exists: `int` by default, `int64_t` if needed

On Windows, things are simpler, and `int` is used all the time. Koffi will throw an error if any enumeration value does not fit in a 32-bit integer.

```js
// For OpenResult, the underlying type will be unsigned int on POSIX, int on Windows
const OpenResult = koffi.enumeration('OpenResult', {
    Success: 0,
    MissingFile: 1,
    AccessDenied: 2,
    OtherError: 3
});

// For RelativePosition, the underlying type will be int everywhere
const RelativePosition = koffi.enumeration('RelativePosition', {
    Left: -1,
    Center: 0,
    Right: 1
});

// For IntLimits, the underlying type will be int64_t on POSIX, and fail on Windows
const Int64Limits = koffi.enumeration('Int64Limits', {
    Min: -9223372036854775808n,
    Max: 9223372036854775807n
});
```

> [!WARNING]
> This behavior may not match your compiler:
>
> - On POSIX platforms, GCC and Clang will use a short integer type if `-fshort-enums` is specified and the enumeration values fit in `short` or `unsigned short`.
> - On Windows, MSVC (and Clang) always use `int` even if some values do not fit, which matches what Koffi does... unless the compiler flag `/Zc:enumTypes` is set, maybe.
>
> Use an explicit type specifier to work around these problems, as shown below.

You can access the constants in `values` member of the type object.

```js
console.log(OpenResult.values.MissingFile); // Prints 1
console.log(RelativePosition.values.Left); // Prints -1
```

You can specify the storage type explicitly as the last argument: `koffi.enumeration(name, values, type)`.

```js
// This one explictly uses int64_t as the underlying type, despite the fact that the values fit inside an int.
const ExplicitEnum = koffi.enumeration('ExplicitEnum', {
    Zero: 0,
    One: 1,
    Two: 2
}, 'int64_t');
```

## Generic decode function

Use `koffi.decode()` to decode the data pointed to by a pointer (represented by a BigInt value).

Some arguments are optional and this function can be called in several ways:

- `koffi.decode(ptr, type)`: no offset
- `koffi.decode(ptr, offset, type)`: explicit offset to add to the pointer before decoding

By default, Koffi expects NUL terminated strings when decoding them. See below if you need to specify the string length.

The following example illustrates how to decode an integer and a C string variable.

```c
int my_int = 42;
const char *my_string = "foobar";
```

```js
const my_int = lib.symbol('my_int');
const my_string = lib.symbol('my_string');

console.log(koffi.decode(my_int, 'int')) // Prints 42
console.log(koffi.decode(my_string, 'const char *')) // Prints "foobar"
```

There is also an optional ending `length` argument that you can use in two cases:

- Use it to give the number of bytes to decode in non-NUL terminated strings: `koffi.decode(ptr, 'char *', 5)`
- Decode consecutive values into an array. For example, here is how you can decode an array with 3 float values: `koffi.decode(ptr, 'float', 3)`. This is equivalent to `koffi.decode(ptr, koffi.array('float', 3))`.

The example below will decode the symbol `my_string` defined above but only the first three bytes.

```js
// Only decode 3 bytes from the C string my_string
console.log(koffi.decode(my_string, 'const char *', 3)) // Prints "foo"
```

# Encode to C memory

Use `koffi.encode()` to encode JS values into C symbols or pointers, which are represented by BigInt numbers.

Some arguments are optional and this function can be called in several ways:

- `koffi.encode(ptr, type, value)`: no offset
- `koffi.encode(ptr, offset, type, value)`: explicit offset to add to the pointer before encoding

We'll reuse the examples shown above and change the variable values with `koffi.encode()`.

```c
int my_int = 42;
const char *my_string = NULL;
```

```js
const my_int = lib.symbol('my_int');
const my_string = lib.symbol('my_string');

console.log(koffi.decode(my_int, 'int')) // Prints 42
console.log(koffi.decode(my_string, 'const char *')) // Prints null

koffi.encode(my_int, 'int', -1);
koffi.encode(my_string, 'const char *', 'Hello World!');

console.log(koffi.decode(my_int, 'int')) // Prints -1
console.log(koffi.decode(my_string, 'const char *')) // Prints "Hello World!"
```

When encoding strings (either directly or embedded in arrays or structs), the memory will be bound to the raw pointer value and managed by Koffi. You can assign to the same string again and again without any leak or risk of use-after-free.

There is also an optional ending `length` argument that you can use to encode an array. For example, here is how you can encode an array with 3 float values: `koffi.encode(symbol, 'float', [1, 2, 3], 3)`. This is equivalent to `koffi.encode(symbol, koffi.array('float', 3), [1, 2, 3])`.
